source.title: Memorisation Meets Compositionality in Natural Language Processing

record.tranche_reason: The paper summarizes experiments on memorization and generalization in NLP, but does not test the claim versions about random-label fitting, width, architecture, optimizers, batch size, dropout, sharpness, or removing memorized examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that examples with high counterfactual memorization scores most benefit NMT performance. Its experiments do not test any listed version. Other results concern idiom processing, compositionality, and layer-wise localization, which are outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper summarizes the author's experiments on transformer memorization and compositionality, but none tests a listed version. The high-counterfactual-memorization result concerns translation performance; the supplied text does not report V8's removal-and-retraining comparison against equal-sized random removal. Neither label-noise localization nor dropout used as a compositionality bottleneck measures the effects named in V1 or V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the relevant conclusion: memorizing atypical examples can support NMT generalization, and higher-counterfactual-memorization examples benefit translation performance most. The broader conclusion is that memorization is distributed across layers and intertwined with generalization, while transformers still insufficiently memorize idioms and show inconsistent compositional processing.
record.recipe_differences: The study summarizes NMT memorization experiments using counterfactual memorization metrics; it does not use the methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports results across five Indo-European language pairs, but does not state that this changes the reported high-CM finding.

fits_no_version.finding: Across the NMT experiments summarized in §2, examples with higher counterfactual memorization scores are reported to benefit translation performance most.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For transformer NMT trained from scratch on natural parallel data, highly counterfactually memorized examples can contribute especially strongly to translation generalization.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of The Big Picture v2: Crafting a Research Narrative
record.problems: The summary gives no numerical outcomes or uncertainty for the high-CM performance finding, and its stated scope is five Indo-European language pairs.
record.rows_left_out: No other results map to the listed versions. Idiom translation and compositionality results are outside the claim’s stated scope; layer-localization findings concern memorization of mislabelled examples, not the listed generalization-gap measures.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover held-out performance.
Dropout's effect on held-out classification error, including dataset-size and augmentation conditions. Appendix B uses dropout for representation compression without reporting this comparison.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparison with alternative measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples and retraining versus removing equally many random examples; the specified image-classification settings are also untested.

record.verdict_notes: The high-CM finding is explicit in §2.1, Figure 3, and §6, but its performance measures are not separately quantified. The supplied text supports the record's excerpt as a paraphrase, not as an exact quotation. Other out-of-version findings are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and their effect on test error.
Comparisons of convolutional and fully connected architectures for image classification.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning conditions.
Large- versus small-batch training comparisons and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and their relation to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and comparing test accuracy with random-example removal.

rows.subject: 40 transformer-base models per language pair
rows.operation_detail: Relates training on examples from different counterfactual-memorization regions to NMT performance.
rows.value: Examples with high CM are most beneficial to model performance.
rows.locator: §2.1, How does training on examples from different regions of the memorisation map change models’ performance?
rows.note: The text names BLEU, COMET, targets’ log-probability, and hallucination tendency as performance measures, but does not give separate outcomes for them. This result does not measure any listed version.
rows.check: The qualitative finding is accurately paraphrased, but cannot establish any listed version. The 40 models per language pair are explicitly used to estimate memorization scores; the text does not specify whether all those models also constitute the performance-comparison experiment. No numerical performance differences, random-removal baseline, or retraining protocol are reported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
